nm_a_north_end_routes.blurb: The first stretch of cliff you meet on the walk in at the Rough and Ready Hills, a volcanic ridge west of Las Cruces. Eleven lines here, mostly bolted with a few trad or top-rope options, running from easy 5.7 up to a single 5.11, with the bulk sitting between 5.7 and 5.10. A couple of routes share anchors, which makes the wall handy for top-roping. Most lines pick up two or three stars. Because the wall sits right beside a gap in the hills, it catches a lot of wind, so bring a layer on blustery days. A friendly place for a warm-up or for newer leaders.

nm_full_moon_wall.blurb: A bolted sport wall on the east side of Luna Park, in the Red Rock Arroyo near Truth or Consequences. All eleven routes are sport, with a spread from 5.7 up to a pair of low 5.12s; the middle of the range, around 5.9 and 5.10, holds most of the lines. The wall looks south, and it works best for morning and late-afternoon sessions rather than the midday heat. A short trail past the pit toilet leads downhill to the base. Moderate face and slot lines make it a good stop for a mixed group.

nm_grandstand_the.blurb: A small cliff in Pecos River Canyon, east of Santa Fe, set among pines above the river in the canyon's pink granite. Eleven routes, nine of them bolted and two on trad gear, and the grades start at 5.9 and climb to 5.12, with 5.10 and 5.11 making up most of the list. A steep roof line is the standout and draws visitors on its own. The setting is pleasant, with a handful of other fun lines nearby. This is more of an intermediate and hard-leader wall than a beginner spot.

nm_keep_the_2.blurb: A free-standing sandstone boulder in Upper Mesteño Canyon near Roy, one of the few detached blocks in the canyon. Eleven problems range from VB up to V8, though most fall in the V0 to V2 band with a few harder tests. The uphill face gives easy highballs on solid stone, while the downhill face is shorter and steeper on rock that is less reliable. The sandstone here is fragile, so treat it gently. A short scramble through scrub oak past the big roof boulder gets you there.

nm_3_gold_rush_wall.blurb: One of the seven walls of Vista Verde Crag, a long basalt band above the Rio Grande Gorge southwest of Taos. This section is a run of steep dihedrals and aretes strung together, with eleven routes: nine sport and two trad. Grades begin at 5.10 and reach 5.12, and the majority are 5.10. The cliff band as a whole faces east, giving strong morning sun and cooler afternoons in summer. Lines are up to roughly a rope length, so expect sustained, pocketed basalt climbing and views over the gorge. Bring a helmet.

nm_cragacito.blurb: A compact sport crag on the north side of the river in the Upper East Fork, in the Jemez Mountains, a short walk upstream of the Amphitheater. All eleven routes are bolted and fall in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with nine of them at 5.11. The climbing mixes faces, cracks, bulges and small roofs, so styles vary from stemming to powerful moves over overhangs. It slips into shade early in the afternoon, which suits hot days. Several lines link up well, and a few need a stick clip for the opening bolt. Not for beginners.

nm_sleeping_beauty_wall.blurb: A squared-out alcove just up and left of the main Enchanted Tower, in the Datil area at roughly 8,000 feet. The middle of the wall overhangs, and the eleven climbs are almost all sport (one is trad), from 5.7 to 5.11. Six of them are 5.11, so it favors strong leaders, though a few easier lines are on offer. Holds run from big jugs on some routes to tiny crimps on others. It is a popular wall, so expect other parties in peak season. You can walk to the base along slope trails from either side.

nm_west_face.blurb: The busiest face of Mushroom Boulder, a mega-moderate block beside the road in Mills Canyon at Roy, in northeast New Mexico. It holds eleven problems, the most of any face on the boulder, with grades from V1 up to V7 and a good cluster around V3 to V5. Because it is so close to the road, the walk is only a couple of minutes, and the boulder is a handy warm-up when the day is cold. Roy is most comfortable from mid-fall to mid-spring, since summers run hot.

_conflicts.nm_west_face: Stored rock is shale; Mountain Project describes the Roy boulders (including Mushroom Boulder's West Face) as sandstone: https://www.mountainproject.com/area/121731910/mushroom-boulder and https://www.mountainproject.com/area/116551105/roy
_conflicts.nm_a_north_end_routes: Stored rock is rhyolite; Mountain Project describes the Rough and Ready Hills rock as volcanic tuff: https://www.mountainproject.com/area/106379854/rough-and-ready-hills
